metadata.hardware_requirements: The training process, presented in Figure 8, can be finished in less than 24 hours on a computing server with NVIDIA Quadro K620 GPU and Intel Xeon CPU E5-1650 (3.6 GHz, 6 cores).

nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering. The data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.
nodes_source.description: Traffic video data from which vehicle locations are extracted and reformed as position matrices, used as input for the DRL method. This 'real-world traffic data' also formed the basis for simulation experiments, and was used as 'empirical data' to calibrate simulation parameters for driving behaviors.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Available from the corresponding author upon request; no public URL or DOI provided.

nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames and formatted as position matrices for input into the DRL method.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=2, no specific tools or parameters stated for extraction.

nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state st: St = {mt-(N-1),..., mt}. For computation efficiency, down-sampling is introduced before the matrix stack to reduce the input dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.
nodes_process.description: Consecutive position matrices from N time steps are stacked to form a state representation. Down-sampling is applied for computational efficiency to reduce input dimensions while preserving vehicle position information.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, 1/1 param stated (N=3 from Table 1's 'State matrix dimension'), but down-sampling method unspecified.

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: A deep neural network, specifically a Q-network, is defined to approximate the action-value function Q*(s,a). It's a revised version of Mnih et al.'s Q-network, consisting of three CNN layers and one FC layer per output.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all architecture details from Figure 7 provided.

nodes_process.node_name: Train DRL Q-network with multitask learning
nodes_process.source_quote: The gradient-based algorithm Adam [28] is used to update wi to minimize the loss function. The experience replay [30] stores the data prepared for training into the replay buffer and samples these data uniformly for training the agent. The target network [29] is introduced for a stable estimation of target value Q*(s, a). A multitask learning strategy is implemented in the training process to improve learning efficiency.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network is trained using a deep Q-learning algorithm with several stabilization techniques: experience replay, a target network, and a multitask learning strategy to predict mean speed and queue length simultaneously. The Adam algorithm minimizes the loss function.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, Adam named, most parameters stated from Table 1, but discount factor gamma value is missing.

nodes_process.node_name: Evaluate DRL model in microscopic traffic simulation
nodes_process.source_quote: A series of simulation experiments based on real-world traffic data are conducted to evaluate the proposed approach. The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31].
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is evaluated through simulation experiments using the SUMO microscopic traffic simulator, based on real-world traffic data from a freeway in Qingdao, China. The simulation covers 7:50 a.m. to 9:00 a.m.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO named, all parameters stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering
nodes_process.description: A baseline scenario is evaluated where no ramp metering is applied, operating within the same SUMO simulation environment and traffic data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO named, no additional parameters.

nodes_process.source_quote: the second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method. The ramp metering rate rk for k-th cycle is given by the following: rk = rk-1 + KR[ok - ô] - Kp[ok-1 - ok]. ô refers to the desired value for mainline occupancy, which is set to 16% in this study. KR = 90 and Kp = 50 are two regulator parameters in PI-ALINEA
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA ramp metering method is evaluated as a second baseline. It calculates the ramp metering rate based on previous red phase length and current/previous downstream occupancies, with fixed green phase length and specific regulator parameters.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO named, all parameters stated.

nodes_process.node_name: Compare DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control performance
nodes_process.source_quote: The results demonstrate that, in comparison with a state-of-the-practice method, the proposed DRL method results in (1) lower travel times in the mainline, (2) shorter vehicle queues at the on-ramp, and (3) higher traffic flows downstream of the merging area.
nodes_process.description: The performance of the DRL method is compared against the PI-ALINEA method and a no-control baseline across various metrics, including travel times, queue lengths, and traffic flows. Perturbation analysis is also conducted to evaluate the impact of information from different subareas.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard metrics, no additional tools or parameters.
